etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English long, lang, from Old English long, lang (“long, tall, lasting”), from Proto-West Germanic *lang, from Proto-Germanic *langaz (“long”), from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos (“long”).

Cognate with Scots lang (“long”), North Frisian long, lung (“long”), Saterland Frisian loang (“long”), Norwegian, West Frisian, Dutch and German lang (“long”), Swedish lång (“long”), Icelandic langur (“long”), Portuguese longo (“long”), Spanish luengo (“long”), French long, Latin longus (“long”), Russian дли́нный (dlínnyj), до́лго (dólgo), Sanskrit दीर्घ (dīrgha, “long”).

The word exceptionally retains the Old English darkening of -a- before nasals. Though there are other such examples in Middle and Modern English (e.g. bond, song, throng, wrong), the o-form may have been reinforced by Old French long, from Latin longus, from the same Indo-European word. Doublet of lungo and lunge.

definitions.definition: Specifically, having much distance in a horizontal dimension (see also Usage Notes below).
Travelling a great distance.
(informal) Having a long penis.
Having much distance in space from one end to the other.

definitions.definition: (of weapons fire, landing aircraft, etc.) Passing or landing ahead of or beyond the intended target or location.

quote.citation: 2021 March 10, Drachinifel, 28:10 from the start, in Guadalcanal Campaign - The Big Night Battle: Night 1 (IJN 3(?) : 2 USN)‎[1], archived from the original on 7 November 2022:
quote.text: Juneau was making good time with the other surviving U.S. Navy ships, despite her damage, when the I-26 spotted her and sent a salvo of Type 95 torpedoes in her direction.  Passing between the Helena and San Francisco, some indication being they had actually been shot at the San Francisco and gone long because San Francisco was travelling significantly slower than expected, they nonetheless hit Juneau and detonated the ship’s magazine.

definitions.definition: (sports, of a ball or shot) Going beyond the intended target.
Travelling or extending too great a distance in space.
Having great duration.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter II, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: I had occasion […] to make a somewhat long business trip to Chicago, and on my return  […]  I found Farrar awaiting me in the railway station. He smiled his wonted fraction by way of greeting,  […] , and finally leading me to his buggy, turned and drove out of town. I was completely mystified at such an unusual proceeding.

definitions.definition: Seeming to last a lot of time, due to being boring, tedious, tiring, irksome, etc.

quote.citation: [1877], Anna Sewell, “A Strike for Liberty”, in Black Beauty: […], London: Jarrold and Sons, […], →OCLC, part II, page 109:
quote.text: What I suffered with that rein for four long months in my lady’s carriage, it would be hard to describe, but I am quite sure that, had it lasted much longer, either my health or my temper would have given way.

definitions.definition: (UK, Ireland, dated) Not short; tall.

quote.text: Bless ’em all, bless ’em all, the long, the short and the tall.

definitions.definition: (finance) Possessing or owning stocks, bonds, commodities, or other financial instruments with the aim of benefiting from an expected rise in their value.
(cricket) Of a fielding position, close to the boundary (or closer to the boundary than the equivalent short position).
(gambling) Of betting odds, offering a very large return for a small wager.
Occurring or coming after an extended interval; distant in time; far away.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IIII, Canto IIII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], part II (books IV–VI), London:  […]  [Richard Field] for William Ponsonby, →OCLC, page 55:

definitions.definition: (linguistics) A long vowel.

quote.citation: 1877, Henry Sweet, A Handbook of Phonetics, volume 2, page 60:
quote.text: In French most vowels are half-long, and are only occasionally lengthened or shortened into full longs and shorts.

definitions.definition: (prosody) A long syllable.
(music) A note formerly used in music, one half the length of a large, twice that of a breve.
(programming) A long integer variable, twice the size of an int, two or four times the size of a short, and half of a long long.
(finance) An entity with a long position in an asset; for example, a trader or investor possessing an amount of a company's shares.
(finance) A long-maturity security, such as a ten- or twenty-year bond.

quote.citation: 1977, Jerome B. Cohen, Edward D. Zinbarg, Arthur Zeikel, Guide to Intelligent Investing, →OCLC, page 203:
quote.text: Likewise, if borrowers prefer to sell short-maturity issues at the time lenders prefer to invest in longs, as is the case when interest rates are expected to fall, longer maturity issues will tend to yield less than shorter maturity issues.

quote.citation: "U.S. Treasury Market Structure", https://www.mfaalts.org/issue/u-s-treasury-market-structure/
quote.text: Hedge funds are constrained in how much leverage they can utilize, in part because the futures contracts they are shorting against their Treasury longs have significant initial margin requirements.

definitions.definition: (Oxbridge, dated) Clipping of long vacation (“summer vacation”).

quote.text: “ […]  Did I not forbid all these nicknames and all this Oxfordish, by proclamation, last Long.”“Last Long?”“Hem! last protracted vacation.”

definitions.definition: (transitive, finance) To take a long position in.

quote.text: The left panel shows the profile of a portfolio consisting of longing a call and shorting a put.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English longe, lange, from Old English longe, lange, from the adjective (see above).

definitions.definition: Over too great a distance, beyond the target.
(chiefly sports) Over a great distance in space.

definitions.definition: (as premodifier of a verb, participle, adjective, preposition, or adverb) For a long time.

quote.citation: 1863 November 19, Abraham Lincoln, Dedicatory Remarks (Gettysburg Address)‎[10], near Soldiers' National Cemetery, →LCCN, Bliss copy, page 2:

quote.citation: 1922, Michael Arlen, “Ep./4/2”, in “Piracy”: A Romantic Chronicle of These Days:
quote.text: The world was awake to the 2nd of May, but Mayfair is not the world, and even the menials of Mayfair lie long abed.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, David Van Tassel, Lee DeHaan, “Wild Plants to the Rescue”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3:
quote.text: Plant breeding is always a numbers game. […] The wild species we use are rich in genetic variation, […]. In addition, we are looking for rare alleles, so the more plants we try, the better. These rarities may be new mutations, or they can be existing ones that are neutral—or are even selected against—in a wild population. A good example is mutations that disrupt seed dispersal, leaving the seeds on the heads long after they are ripe.

definitions.definition: A long time (see usage notes).

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English longen, from Old English langian (“to long for, yearn after, grieve for, be pained, lengthen, grow longer, summon, belong”), from Proto-West Germanic *langōn, from Proto-Germanic *langōną (“to desire, long for”), from Proto-Indo-European *lengʷʰ- (“to be easy, be quick, jump, move around, vary”). Cognate with German langen (“to reach, be sufficient”), Swedish langa (“to push, pass by hand”), Icelandic langa (“to want, desire”), Dutch, German verlangen (“to desire, want, long for”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To await, aspire, desire greatly (something to occur or to be true).

quote.citation: 1922, Margery Williams, The Velveteen Rabbit:
quote.text: The Rabbit sighed. He thought it would be a long time before this magic called Real happened to him. He longed to become Real, to know what it felt like; and yet the idea of growing shabby and losing his eyes and whiskers was rather sad.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English long, lang, an aphetic form of Middle English ilong, ylong, from Old English ġelong, ġelang (“along, belonging, depending, consequent”); the verb later reinterpreted as an aphetic form of belong.

definitions.definition: (archaic) On account of, because of.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, translated by John Florio, Essays, II.8, page 224:
quote.text: I am of opinion, that in regarde of theſe debauches and lewde actions, fathers may, in ſome ſort, be blamed, and that it is onely long of them.

definitions.definition: (archaic) To be appropriate to, to pertain or belong to.

quote.text: A goodly Armour, and full rich aray, / Which long’d to Angela, the Saxon Queene, / All fretted round with gold, and goodly wel beseene.
